cues.text: Simulated model, assumed signs. The legs replay recorded walking kinematics; the brain runs a spiking model whose input is our assumption: activation of P9 descending neurons.
Simulated model: the assumed P9 input spreads through the prow and wedge — shelves where descending neurons collect commands for the nerve cord.
Simulated model: the wave reaches the lateral accessory lobes, premotor hubs that route steering signals toward descending neurons.
Simulated model: the compass neuropils — bridge, ellipsoid body, fan-shaped body — hum along as the fly holds a straight heading.
Simulated model: every spike you see is simulated — the gait is replayed from recordings, but no brain activity was measured.
Simulated model: antennal motion centers stay quiet; our assumed walking scene includes no wind or sound.
Simulated model: the assumed drive holds steady and the simulated pattern loops with the 4-second clip.

qa.a: No. The colors show a simulated model (Shiu et al. 2024) with partly assumed neurotransmitter signs — no spikes were recorded from this fly.

qa.q: Why is the stimulus an assumption?
qa.a: Shiu et al. did not publish a walking stimulus, so we picked a plausible trigger — P9 descending neurons, reported to drive walking (Bidaye et al. 2020).
A leaky integrate-and-fire network built on the FlyWire whole-brain connectome by Shiu et al. 2024. Synapse strengths come from connection counts; excitatory or inhibitory signs are partly assumed.

qa.q: What lights up when the fly walks?
qa.a: In the model, premotor regions — wedge, prow and the lateral accessory lobes — carry activity toward descending neurons that steer the legs.
